mentions.author: rramadass
mentions.text:
Your reasoning is wrong. When at rest the momentum of both balls is zero and when you pull one ball away from the other the change in momentum (and hence the force) is opposite to the other ball. Thus there is no collision and transfer of energy i.e. each is independent.

It is only at the point of collision that the impulsive force is imparted to the other body.

See this Khan Academy video "Impulse and momentum dodgeball example" for detailed understanding: [course]

Also see article "Momentum Change and Impulse Connection" (note the Rebounding Collison section at the bottom) : [link]

mentions.text:

That's irrelevant because it's true of everything. I can also look up and learn quantum mechanics at khan academy:
[course]

Sure it's feasible to look up facts here and there, but it's harder to grasp the underlying meaning and generalize it when rushing to check in code for a job, compared to having dedicated and structured time set aside.

Anecdotally, I started coding intensely in middle school and thought I was pretty bad ass by the I time entered college. Was blown away at how little I knew about what I didn't know. Gave up hubris at that point.

mentions.author: jmc734
mentions.story: Ask HN: What are some good online resources to learn electrical engineering?
mentions.text: This is a good place to start if you aren't already overly familiar with the principle of electromagnetism and circuit theory: [course] After that the progression of a traditional EE education usually goes like this: transient and AC circuit analysis (phasors, Fourier, Laplace), linear systems, opamp and analog filter design, digital logic, some power stuff (3 phase, etc.), active devices (diodes, BJTs, FETs), RF basics. From there, the path usually splits based on your personal interest. Some options are usually power systems, digital systems (embedded systems), digital systems (IC design), AC design (usually mixed with RF).
